🍳 Recipes¶

Use modern Python annotations¶

Target a recent Python version and prefer built-in collection and union syntax in generated types.

Options: --target-python-version, --use-union-operator, --use-standard-collections

Keep validation constraints in type hints¶

Combine Annotated hints with strict scalar handling when downstream tooling reads type metadata.

Options: --use-annotated, --field-constraints, --strict-types

--allof-class-hierarchy¶

Controls how allOf schemas are represented in the generated class hierarchy. --allof-class-hierarchy if-no-conflict (default) creates parent classes for allOf schemas only when there are no property conflicts between parent schemas. Otherwise, properties are merged into the child class which is then decoupled from the parent classes and no longer inherits from them. --allof-class-hierarchy always keeps class hierarchy for allOf schemas, even in multiple inheritance scenarios where two parent schemas define the same property. msgspec.Struct output declares the fields of parent classes whose layouts msgspec cannot combine instead of inheriting from them.

Usage

datamodel-codegen --input allof_root_model_constraints.json --allof-class-hierarchy always # (1)!
  1. --allof-class-hierarchy - the option documented here
Examples

Input Schema:

{
  "$schema": "http://json-schema.org/draft-07/schema#",
  "definitions": {
    "StringDatatype": {
      "description": "A base string type.",
      "type": "string",
      "pattern": "^\\S(.*\\S)?$"
    },
    "ConstrainedStringDatatype": {
      "description": "A constrained string.",
      "allOf": [
        { "$ref": "#/definitions/StringDatatype" },
        { "type": "string", "minLength": 1, "pattern": "^[A-Z].*" }
      ]
    },
    "IntegerDatatype": {
      "description": "A whole number.",
      "type": "integer"
    },
    "NonNegativeIntegerDatatype": {
      "description": "Non-negative integer.",
      "allOf": [
        { "$ref": "#/definitions/IntegerDatatype" },
        { "minimum": 0 }
      ]
    },
    "BoundedIntegerDatatype": {
      "description": "Integer between 0 and 100.",
      "allOf": [
        { "$ref": "#/definitions/IntegerDatatype" },
        { "minimum": 0, "maximum": 100 }
      ]
    },
    "EmailDatatype": {
      "description": "Email with format.",
      "allOf": [
        { "$ref": "#/definitions/StringDatatype" },
        { "format": "email" }
      ]
    },
    "FormattedStringDatatype": {
      "description": "A string with email format.",
      "type": "string",
      "format": "email"
    },
    "ObjectBase": {
      "type": "object",
      "properties": {
        "id": { "type": "integer" }
      }
    },
    "ObjectWithAllOf": {
      "description": "Object inheritance - not a root model.",
      "allOf": [
        { "$ref": "#/definitions/ObjectBase" },
        { "type": "object", "properties": { "name": { "type": "string" } } }
      ]
    },
    "MultiRefAllOf": {
      "description": "Multiple refs - not handled by new code.",
      "allOf": [
        { "$ref": "#/definitions/StringDatatype" },
        { "$ref": "#/definitions/IntegerDatatype" }
      ]
    },
    "NoConstraintAllOf": {
      "description": "No constraints added.",
      "allOf": [
        { "$ref": "#/definitions/StringDatatype" }
      ]
    },
    "IncompatibleTypeAllOf": {
      "description": "Incompatible types.",
      "allOf": [

        { "type": "boolean" }
      ]
    },
    "ConstraintWithProperties": {

    },

      "description": "Number and integer are compatible.",

        { "type": "number", "minimum": 0 }
      ]
    },
    "RefWithSchemaKeywords": {
      "description": "Ref with additional schema keywords.",
      "allOf": [
        { "$ref": "#/definitions/StringDatatype", "minLength": 5 },
        { "maxLength": 100 }
      ]
    },
    "ArrayDatatype": {
      "type": "array",
      "items": { "type": "string" }
    },
    "RefToArrayAllOf": {
      "description": "Ref to array - not a root model.",
      "allOf": [
        { "$ref": "#/definitions/ArrayDatatype" },
        { "minItems": 1 }
      ]
    },
    "ObjectNoPropsDatatype": {
      "type": "object"
    },
    "RefToObjectNoPropsAllOf": {
      "description": "Ref to object without properties - not a root model.",

        { "$ref": "#/definitions/ObjectNoPropsDatatype" },

        { "minLength": 1 }
      ]

    "incompatible": { "$ref": "#/definitions/IncompatibleTypeAllOf" },
    "withprops": { "$ref": "#/definitions/ConstraintWithProperties" },
    "withitems": { "$ref": "#/definitions/ConstraintWithItems" },

    "refobjnoprops": { "$ref": "#/definitions/RefToObjectNoPropsAllOf" },
    "refpatternprops": { "$ref": "#/definitions/RefToPatternPropsAllOf" },
    "refnestedallof": { "$ref": "#/definitions/RefToNestedAllOfAllOf" },

from __future__ import annotations

from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, constr


class Entity(BaseModel):
    type: str
    type_list: list[str] | None = ['playground:Entity']


class Entity2(BaseModel):
    type: str
    type_list: list[str]


class Thing(Entity):
    type: str
    type_list: list[str] | None = ['playground:Thing']
    name: constr(min_length=1) = Field(..., description='The things name')


class Location(Entity2):
    type: str
    type_list: list[str]
    address: constr(min_length=5) = Field(
        ..., description='The address of the location'
    )


class Person(Thing, Location):
    name: constr(min_length=1) = Field(..., description="The person's name")
    type: str
    type_list: list[str]

from typing import Any

from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, constr


class Person(BaseModel):
    name: constr(min_length=1) = Field(..., description='The things name')
    type: Any | None = 'playground:Location'
    type_list: list[Any] | None = [
        'playground:Person',
        'playground:Thing',
        'playground:Location',
    ]
    address: constr(min_length=5) = Field(
        ..., description='The address of the location'
    )

class Entity2(BaseModel):

--allof-merge-mode¶

Merge constraints from root model references in allOf schemas.

The --allof-merge-mode constraints merges only constraint properties (minLength, maximum, etc.) from parent schemas referenced in allOf. This ensures child schemas inherit validation constraints while keeping other properties separate.

Usage

datamodel-codegen --input allof_root_model_constraints.json --allof-merge-mode constraints # (1)!
  1. --allof-merge-mode - the option documented here
Examples

Input Schema:

openapi: "3.0.0"
info:
  title: Test materialize allOf defaults
  version: "1.0.0"
components:
  schemas:
    Parent:
      type: object
      properties:
        name:
          type: string
          default: "parent_default"
          minLength: 1
        count:
          type: integer
          default: 10
          minimum: 0
    Child:
      allOf:
        - $ref: "#/components/schemas/Parent"
        - type: object
          properties:
            name:
              maxLength: 100
            count:
              maximum: 1000

Output:

# generated by datamodel-codegen:
#   filename:  allof_materialize_defaults.yaml
#   timestamp: 2019-07-26T00:00:00+00:00

from __future__ import annotations

from pydantic import BaseModel, conint, constr


class Parent(BaseModel):
    name: constr(min_length=1) | None = 'parent_default'
    count: conint(ge=0) | None = 10


class Child(Parent):
    name: constr(min_length=1, max_length=100) | None = 'parent_default'
    count: conint(ge=0, le=1000) | None = 10

--disable-future-imports¶

Prevent automatic addition of future imports in generated code.

The --disable-future-imports option stops the generator from adding 'from future import annotations' to the output. This is useful when you need compatibility with tools or environments that don't support postponed evaluation of annotations (PEP 563).

See also: Python Version Compatibility

Usage

datamodel-codegen --input keep_model_order_field_references.json --disable-future-imports --target-python-version 3.10 # (1)!
  1. --disable-future-imports - the option documented here

Input Schema:

{
  "$schema": "http://json-schema.org/draft-07/schema#",
  "title": "DescriptionType",
  "type": "object",
  "properties": {
    "metadata": {
      "type": "array",
      "items": {
        "$ref": "#/definitions/Metadata"
      }
    }
  },
  "definitions": {
    "Metadata": {
      "title": "Metadata",
      "type": "object",
      "properties": {
        "title": {
          "type": "string"
        }
      }
    }
  }
}

--enum-field-as-literal¶

Convert all enum fields to Literal types instead of Enum classes.

The --enum-field-as-literal all flag converts all enum types to Literal type annotations. This is useful when you want string literal types instead of Enum classes for all enumerations.

datamodel-codegen --input enums.graphql --enum-field-as-literal all # (1)!

--enum-field-as-literal-map¶

Override enum/literal generation per-field via JSON mapping.

The --enum-field-as-literal-map option allows per-field control over whether to generate Literal types or Enum classes. Overrides --enum-field-as-literal.

You can pass the mapping either inline as JSON or as a path to a JSON file.

Usage

datamodel-codegen --input enum_field_as_literal_map.json --enum-field-as-literal-map '{"status": "literal"}' # (1)!

{
  "$schema": "http://json-schema.org/draft-07/schema#",
  "title": "EnumFieldAsLiteralMap",
  "type": "object",
  "properties": {
    "status": {
      "title": "Status",
      "type": "string",
      "enum": ["active", "inactive", "pending"]
    },
    "priority": {
      "title": "Priority",
      "type": "string",
      "enum": ["high", "medium", "low"]
    },
    "category": {
      "title": "Category",
      "type": "string",
      "enum": ["a", "b", "c"]
    }
  }
}

--filter-literal-values¶

Keep only the values of a const or an enum that meet the constraints beside them.

JSON Schema validates a value against the enum and the keywords beside it, so {"enum": ["hello", "goodbye"], "maxLength": 5} admits hello only. With --filter-literal-values, the Literal or the Enum of a const or an enum holds the values that meet the minLength, maxLength, minimum, maximum, exclusiveMinimum, exclusiveMaximum, multipleOf and pattern keywords beside them, as far as the generator can decide them (a pattern only where every regular expression engine reads it alike). A schema none of whose values meets them admits no value: it stays as written, with a warning. A field that writes a constraint itself, such as Field(min_length=...), keeps the values that constraint checks. --omit-redundant-constraints includes this check. Without the option, every value stays and the keywords are written beside the type.

Usage

datamodel-codegen --input max_items_enum.yaml --filter-literal-values # (1)!
  1. --filter-literal-values - the option documented here
Examples

Input Schema:

openapi: "3.1.0"
components:
  schemas:
    Foo:
      type: object
      properties:
        bar:
          type: array
          items:
            enum:
              - hello
              - goodbye

--ignore-enum-constraints¶

Ignore enum constraints and use base string type instead of Enum classes.

The --ignore-enum-constraints flag ignores enum constraints and uses the base type (str) instead of generating Enum classes. This is useful when you need flexibility in the values a field can accept beyond the defined enum members.

--import-overrides¶

Override modules for generated imports by symbol name.

The mapping applies to imports in generated output regardless of their original module, except for __future__ imports. This is useful for routing typing helpers through a project compatibility module across Python target versions.

Usage

datamodel-codegen --input datetime.json --output-model-type typing.TypedDict --target-python-version 3.10 --import-overrides '{"TypedDict": "my_project.typing_compat", "NotRequired": "my_project.typing_compat"}' # (1)!

Input Schema:

{
  "$schema": "http://json-schema.org/draft-07/schema#",

    "User": {
      "type": "object",
      "properties": {
        "name": {
          "type": "string",
          "example": "ken"
        },
        "birthDay": {
          "type": "string",
          "format": "date-time",
          "example": "2016-08-29T09:12:33.001Z"
        }
      }
    }
  }
}

#   filename:  datetime.json
#   timestamp: 1985-10-26T08:21:00+00:00

from typing import Any, TypeAlias

from my_project.typing_compat import NotRequired, TypedDict

Model: TypeAlias = Any

    name: NotRequired[str]
    birthDay: NotRequired[str]

--intersect-allof-keywords¶

Combine the keywords of every part of an allOf, a $ref with siblings or an override.

JSON Schema applies the members of an allOf, a $ref and the keywords beside it, and a property that overrides an inherited one all at once, so a value must meet every part. Without the option the keyword of the last part wins where the parts disagree: the sibling of a $ref, the overriding property, the last member of an allOf. With --intersect-allof-keywords, the tightest bound of the parts is written (maximum: 10 beside maximum: 20 keeps 10), an enum holds the values every part admits, a type the types every part admits, required the names of every part, and the patterns of the parts are checked together. An allOf of value schemas at a root, an item or a map value is one constraint schema in the same way, and a null member beside a type that excludes null is dropped. Parts that no value meets together keep the earlier merge with a warning.

Usage

datamodel-codegen --input inherited_overrides.json --intersect-allof-keywords # (1)!
  1. --intersect-allof-keywords - the option documented here
Examples

Input Schema:

{
  "$schema": "https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema",
  "title": "Model",
  "type": "object",
  "properties": {
    "c": {
      "$ref": "#/$defs/Child"
    }
  },
  "$defs": {
    "Base": {
      "type": "object",
      "properties": {
        "x": {
          "type": "integer",
          "maximum": 10
        },
        "e": {
          "type": "string",
          "enum": [
            "a",
            "b"
          ]
        },
        "y": {
          "type": "integer",
          "minimum": 0
        }
      }
    },
    "Child": {
      "allOf": [
        {
          "$ref": "#/$defs/Base"
        },
        {
          "type": "object",
          "properties": {
            "x": {
              "maximum": 20
            },
            "e": {
              "enum": [
                "b",
                "c"
              ]
            },
            "y": {
              "maximum": 5
            }
          }
        }
      ]
    }
  }
}

class Base(BaseModel):

--keep-enum-member-values¶

Give an enum class a value base only when it keeps every member value.

--use-specialized-enum (IntEnum, StrEnum) and --use-subclass-enum ((T, Enum)) give an enum class the value type of its schema type as a base. Without this option the base follows the schema type alone, as in 0.86.0, so a member the base changes is written with the changed value: const branches [1, 2.5] make an IntEnum whose 2.5 becomes 2 (rejecting the schema-valid 2.5 and accepting 2), and ['a', 1] under --use-subclass-enum a (str, Enum) holding '1'. With the option such an enum is a plain Enum that keeps the values as written; members the base keeps, as 1.0 in an IntEnum or 1 in a (float, Enum), keep the base. msgspec keeps the 0.86.0 class where it could not decode the plain Enum. A base that cannot hold a member at all, so that the class failed at import ('a' in an IntEnum, a format: byte enum), gives a plain Enum either way.

Usage

datamodel-codegen --input enum_value_base_kinds.json --keep-enum-member-values # (1)!
  1. --keep-enum-member-values - the option documented here
Examples

Input Schema:

{
  "$schema": "http://json-schema.org/draft-07/schema#",
  "title": "EnumValueBaseKinds",
  "type": "object",
  "properties": {
    "str_then_int": {"oneOf": [{"const": "a"}, {"const": 1}]},
    "int_then_str": {"oneOf": [{"const": 1}, {"const": "a"}]},
    "int_then_float": {"oneOf": [{"const": 1}, {"const": 2.5}]},
    "int_then_bool": {"oneOf": [{"const": 1}, {"const": true}]},
    "numbers": {"type": "number", "enum": [1, 2.5]},
    "integral_floats": {"type": "integer", "enum": [1.0, 2.0]},
    "base64": {"type": "string", "format": "byte", "enum": ["YQ==", "Yg=="]},
    "byte_counts": {"type": "string", "format": "byte", "enum": [1, 2]}
  }
}

--read-const-beside-enum¶

Read a const beside an enum as JSON Schema does.

A const that admits some but not all values of the enum beside it narrows the schema to the admitted values, while the enum class keeps every value as written. With --read-const-beside-enum, a value whose schema names such an enum, a property, an item, a map value or key, a union branch or a $ref to a definition, is typed by the const: Literal[<Enum>.<member>] when the members of the enum equal their values (IntEnum, StrEnum, --use-subclass-enum), the const's own Literal, or None for a null const. A plain Enum, and any msgspec enum, keeps the enum type and warns once per schema location that the other values are accepted. A schema whose const is none of its enum values admits no value and is generated as written with a warning. Under --use-single-value-enum-as-const, an enum that admits the const beside it, such as {"enum": ["a", "b"], "const": "a"}, is read as that const without the enum class written beside it otherwise, except one with nullable: true and a const other than null. Without the option, a const beside an enum is ignored.

Usage

datamodel-codegen --input enum_const_positions.json --read-const-beside-enum # (1)!
  1. --read-const-beside-enum - the option documented here
Examples

Input Schema:

{
  "$schema": "https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema",
  "title": "Positions",
  "type": "object",
  "properties": {
    "property": {"type": "string", "enum": ["a", "b"], "const": "a"},
    "propertySingle": {"type": "string", "enum": ["a"], "const": "a"},
    "words": {"type": "array", "items": {"type": "string", "enum": ["a", "b"], "const": "b"}},
    "counts": {"type": "object", "additionalProperties": {"type": "integer", "enum": [1, 2, 3], "const": 2}},
    "branch": {"anyOf": [{"type": "string", "enum": ["a", "b"], "const": "a"}, {"type": "integer"}]},
    "refSibling": {"$ref": "#/$defs/Switch", "const": "on"},
    "keys": {"type": "object", "propertyNames": {"enum": ["a", "b"], "const": "a"}, "additionalProperties": {"type": "integer"}},
    "refKeys": {"type": "object", "propertyNames": {"$ref": "#/$defs/Narrowed"}, "additionalProperties": {"type": "integer"}},
    "definition": {"$ref": "#/$defs/Narrowed"},
    "definitionSingle": {"$ref": "#/$defs/Single"},
    "allOfDefinition": {"$ref": "#/$defs/AllOfNarrowed"},
    "besideNull": {"$ref": "#/$defs/BesideNull"},
    "constNull": {"$ref": "#/$defs/ConstNull"}
  },

      "type": "string",
      "enum": ["a", "b", "c"],
      "const": "b",
      "x-enum-varnames": ["ALPHA", "BRAVO", "CHARLIE"],
      "x-enum-descriptions": ["First.", "Second.", "Third."]
    },
    "Single": {"type": "string", "enum": ["a"], "const": "a"},
    "AllOfNarrowed": {"allOf": [{"type": "string", "enum": ["a", "b"], "const": "b"}]},
    "BesideNull": {"type": "string", "enum": ["a", null, "b"], "const": "b", "x-enum-varnames": ["ALPHA", "BRAVO"]},
    "ConstNull": {"type": "string", "enum": ["a", null, "b"], "const": null}

    off = 'off'

    off = 'off'

    BRAVO = 'b'
    CHARLIE = 'c'

    a = 'a'
    b = 'b'

    BRAVO = 'b'

--read-unevaluated-properties¶

Read a schema-valued unevaluatedProperties as additionalProperties.

Where no applicator (allOf, anyOf, oneOf, not, if, dependentSchemas, dependencies or a reference) evaluates a property of the object in place, the keys unevaluatedProperties evaluates are exactly those that additionalProperties would, so its schema types the extra keys of a model (__pydantic_extra__: Dict[str, str]) and makes an object without properties a map (RootModel[dict[str, int]]). The schema object as written decides: the models built from its branches keep the extra keys untyped where its applicators evaluate properties. Without the option the extra keys are allowed untyped, as in 0.86.0.

Usage

datamodel-codegen --input unevaluated_properties_schema.json --read-unevaluated-properties # (1)!
  1. --read-unevaluated-properties - the option documented here
Examples

Input Schema:

{
    "$id": "https://example.com/test.schema.json",
    "title": "Resource",
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {
        "name": { "type": "string" }
    },
    "required": ["name"],
    "unevaluatedProperties": {
        "type": "string"
    }
}

--strict-types¶

Enable strict type validation for specified Python types.

The --strict-types option enforces stricter type checking by preventing implicit type coercion for the specified types (str, bytes, int, float, bool). This generates StrictStr, StrictBytes, StrictInt, StrictFloat, and StrictBool types in Pydantic models, ensuring values match exactly without automatic conversion.

See also: Type Mappings and Custom Types

datamodel-codegen --input strict_types.json --strict-types str bytes int float bool # (1)!

--type-overrides¶

Replace schema model types with custom Python types via JSON mapping.

This option is useful for importing models from external libraries (like geojson-pydantic) instead of generating them.

Override Formats:

Format Description
{"ModelName": "package.Type"} Model-level: Skip generation; replace field and inheritance refs
{"Model.field": "package.Type"} Scoped: Override only specific field in specific model

Common Use Cases:

Use Case Example Override
GeoJSON types {"Feature": "geojson_pydantic.Feature"}
Custom datetime {"Timestamp": "pendulum.DateTime"}
MongoDB ObjectId {"ObjectId": "bson.ObjectId"}
Custom validators {"Email": "my_app.types.ValidatedEmail"}

Usage

datamodel-codegen --input type_overrides_test.json --type-overrides '{"CustomType": "my_app.types.CustomType"}' # (1)!
  1. --type-overrides - the option documented here

Model-level overrides skip generation

When you specify a model-level override (without a dot in the key), the generator will skip generating that model entirely and import it from the specified package instead. References to that model are replaced in field annotations and allOf inheritance base classes.

Examples

Input Schema:

{
    "$schema": "http://json-schema.org/draft-07/schema#",
    "definitions": {
        "CustomType": {"type": "string"},
        "User": {
            "type": "object",
            "properties": {
                "id": {"type": "integer"},
                "custom": {"$ref": "#/definitions/CustomType"}
            }
        }
    }
}

from my_app.types import CustomType
from pydantic import BaseModel, RootModel


class Model(RootModel[Any]):
    root: Any


class User(BaseModel):

--use-annotated¶

Use typing.Annotated for Field() with constraints.

The --use-annotated flag generates Field definitions using typing.Annotated syntax instead of default values. This also enables --field-constraints.

--use-annotated alone does not preserve uniqueItems: true as set semantics. Use --use-unique-items-as-set when you need the generated type to enforce uniqueness for array schemas.

Related: --field-constraints

See also: Python Version Compatibility

    height: Annotated[int | float | None, Field(ge=1.0, le=300.0)] = None
    weight: Annotated[float | int | None, Field(ge=1.0, le=1000.0)] = None
    age: Annotated[int | None, Field(gt=0, le=200)] = None
    rating: Annotated[float | None, Field(gt=0.0, le=5.0)] = None


class Users(RootModel[list[User]]):
    root: list[User]


class Id(RootModel[str]):
    root: str


class Rules(RootModel[list[str]]):
    root: list[str]


class Error(BaseModel):
    code: int
    message: str


class Api(BaseModel):
    apiKey: Annotated[
        str | None, Field(description='To be used as a dataset parameter value')
    ] = None
    apiVersionNumber: Annotated[
        str | None, Field(description='To be used as a version parameter value')
    ] = None
    apiUrl: Annotated[
        AnyUrl | None, Field(description="The URL describing the dataset's fields")
    ] = None
    apiDocumentationUrl: Annotated[
        AnyUrl | None, Field(description='A URL to the API console for each API')
    ] = None


class Apis(RootModel[list[Api]]):
    root: list[Api]


class Event(BaseModel):
    name: str | None = None


class Result(BaseModel):
    event: Event | None = None

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Annotated, Literal

from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
from typing_extensions import TypeAliasType

Boolean = TypeAliasType("Boolean", bool)
"""
The `Boolean` scalar type represents `true` or `false`.
"""


String = TypeAliasType("String", str)
"""
The `String` scalar type represents textual data, represented as UTF-8 character sequences. The String type is most often used by GraphQL to represent free-form human-readable text.
"""


class A(BaseModel):
    field: String
    listField: list[String]
    listListField: list[list[String]]
    listOptionalField: list[String | None]
    optionalField: String | None = None
    optionalListField: list[String] | None = None
    optionalListOptionalField: list[String | None] | None = None
    typename__: Annotated[Literal['A'] | None, Field(alias='__typename')] = 'A'

--use-single-dict-for-object-maps¶

Type an object map as one dict instead of a union of dicts.

An object map is an object without properties whose keys patternProperties or propertyNames constrain. With --use-single-dict-for-object-maps it is one dict whose key pattern joins every pattern and whose value is the union of their value types, so an object that mixes the keys of several patterns is accepted; a dict that cannot express the object exactly (keys outside the patterns, different value schemas) is named by a warning. The null and the other types of a type array, such as [object, string, null], join the dict in a union, and its property counts stay on the dict; the dict root model of an object without properties, such as a nullable additionalProperties map, takes the same null. The stricter pattern-map checks of --generate-schema-validators are under --check-pattern-maps-strictly. Without --use-single-dict-for-object-maps the map is written as in 0.86.0: a union of dicts, one per value type of the patterns, the other types of a type array left out; msgspec, which cannot decode a union of several dicts, gets the one dict.

Usage

datamodel-codegen --input pattern_properties_merge.json --output-model-type pydantic_v2.BaseModel --use-single-dict-for-object-maps # (1)!
  1. --use-single-dict-for-object-maps - the option documented here

{
  "$schema": "https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema",
  "type": "object",
  "patternProperties": {
    "^i-": {
      "type": "string"
    },
    "^t-": {
      "type": "string"
    },
    "^n-": {
      "type": "integer"
    }
  }
}

--use-single-value-enum-as-const¶

Treat enum with a single value as const with that value.

JSON Schema defines {"enum": ["low"]} as equal to {"const": "low"}. With --use-single-value-enum-as-const, each schema in the JSON Schema, OpenAPI and AsyncAPI documents whose enum lists one value is read as that const, so the output is the same as for the documents written with const, while the enums that allOf intersections leave stay enums: oneOf/anyOf branches of single-value enums, as Rust's schemars writes documented unit variants, become one Enum with branch titles as member names when there are two or more and all hold values of one JSON type; otherwise each branch is typed as written, such as Literal['a'] | None for one value beside a null branch or Literal['a'] | Literal[1] for values of different JSON types. A schema with one enum value is typed Literal[...] instead of a one-member Enum, except one with nullable: true and a value other than null, which keeps its enum and is read as written. The option reads const branches the same way, which without it merge into one Enum in those cases too. Instance data such as default and examples, extension values (x-... except x-propertyNames), links and servers stay as written, so a schema kept under an extension key, such as one referenced as headers.yaml#/x-rate, is read as written too. A document parsed with draft-04 schema features, which have no const, is kept, and Avro, Protocol Buffers, XML Schema and GraphQL inputs are not changed.

Usage

datamodel-codegen --input schema.json --use-single-value-enum-as-const # (1)!
  1. --use-single-value-enum-as-const - the option documented here
Examples

Input Schema:

{
  "$schema": "https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema",
  "title": "Settings",
  "type": "object",
  "x-meta": {"enum": ["kept"]},
  "properties": {
    "level": {"$ref": "#/$defs/Level"},
    "phase": {"$ref": "#/$defs/Phase"},
    "code": {"$ref": "#/$defs/Code"},

    },
    "version": {"type": "integer", "enum": [2], "default": 2},
    "default": {"type": "string", "enum": ["named"]},
    "both": {"type": "string", "enum": ["same"], "const": "same"},
    "options": {
      "type": "object",
      "additionalProperties": true,
      "default": {"enum": ["kept"]},
      "examples": [{"enum": ["kept"]}]
    },
    "pick": {"$ref": "#/$defs/Pick"}
  },
  "required": ["method"],
  "x-generator": {"name": "schemars", "enum": ["kept"]},
  "$defs": {
    "Level": {
      "description": "How much effort to spend.",
      "oneOf": [
        {"type": "string", "enum": ["low"], "description": "Low effort."},
        {"type": "string", "enum": ["high"], "description": "High effort."}
      ]
    },

--use-specialized-enum¶

Generate StrEnum/IntEnum for string/integer enums (Python 3.11+).

The --use-specialized-enum flag generates specialized enum types: - StrEnum for string enums - IntEnum for integer enums

This is the default behavior for Python 3.11+ targets.

Related: --no-use-specialized-enum, --use-subclass-enum

Option relationships:

  • Requires: --target-python-version = 3.11+ - --use-specialized-enum requires --target-python-version 3.11 or higher.

--use-standard-collections¶

Use built-in dict/list instead of typing.Dict/List.

The --use-standard-collections flag generates built-in container types (dict, list) instead of typing module equivalents. This produces cleaner code for Python 3.10+ where built-in types support subscripting.

Related: --use-generic-container-types

See also: Python Version Compatibility

--use-standard-primitive-types¶

Use Python standard library types for string formats instead of str.

The --use-standard-primitive-types flag configures the code generation to use Python standard library types (UUID, IPv4Address, IPv6Address, Path) for corresponding string formats instead of plain str. This affects dataclass, msgspec, and TypedDict output types. Pydantic already uses these types by default.

Related: --output-datetime-class, --output-model-type

Usage

datamodel-codegen --input use_standard_primitive_types.json --output-model-type dataclasses.dataclass --use-standard-primitive-types # (1)!
  1. --use-standard-primitive-types - the option documented here

  "$schema": "http://json-schema.org/draft-07/schema#",
  "type": "object",
  "properties": {
    "id": {
      "type": "string",
      "format": "uuid"
    },
    "ip_address": {
      "type": "string",
      "format": "ipv4"

      "format": "path"

--use-total-false-for-typed-dict¶

--use-tuple-for-closed-arrays¶

Generate tuple types for positional arrays that no other item can follow.

A prefixItems array whose tail is closed by items: false, unevaluatedItems: false, a false position or contains, and an items array closed by additionalItems: false or a false position, is written as a tuple when its length bounds fix its length, so every position keeps its own type. Without the option only equal minItems and maxItems make a tuple, and a closed array is a list with length constraints that accepts items in the wrong positions. When bounds other than equal minItems and maxItems fix the length, the list stays if its item schemas (the allowed positions and the items schema) accept the same values, compared without annotations and x- keys, with a $ref read as its target and type: [T] as type: T. --use-tuple-for-fixed-items still decides whether the items array form is read. A tuple cannot hold uniqueItems: with --use-unique-items-as-set it stays a tuple and a warning names the field generated without uniqueness, unless --generate-schema-validators checks it.

Usage

datamodel-codegen --input prefix_items_closed_length.json --use-tuple-for-closed-arrays # (1)!

--use-tuple-for-fixed-items¶

Generate tuple types for arrays with items array syntax.

When --use-tuple-for-fixed-items is enabled and an array has items as an array with minItems == maxItems == len(items), generate a tuple type instead of a list.

Usage

datamodel-codegen --input items_array_tuple.json --use-tuple-for-fixed-items # (1)!

--use-tuple-for-fixed-length-arrays¶

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Literal, Union

from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
from typing_extensions import TypeAliasType

Boolean = TypeAliasType("Boolean", bool)
"""
The `Boolean` scalar type represents `true` or `false`.
"""


Int = TypeAliasType("Int", int)
"""
The `Int` scalar type represents non-fractional signed whole numeric values. Int can represent values between -(2^31) and 2^31 - 1.
"""


SimpleString = TypeAliasType("SimpleString", str)


String = TypeAliasType("String", str)
"""
The `String` scalar type represents textual data, represented as UTF-8 character sequences. The String type is most often used by GraphQL to represent free-form human-readable text.
"""


class Person(BaseModel):
    age: Int
    name: String
    typename__: Literal['Person'] | None = Field('Person', alias='__typename')


class Pet(BaseModel):
    name: String
    type: String
    typename__: Literal['Pet'] | None = Field('Pet', alias='__typename')


UnionType = TypeAliasType(
    "UnionType",
    Union[
        'Person',
        'Pet',
    ],
)


class ModelWithTypeAliasField(BaseModel):
    simple_field: SimpleString | None = None
    string_field: String | None = None
    union_field: UnionType | None = None
    typename__: Literal['ModelWithTypeAliasField'] | None = Field(
        'ModelWithTypeAliasField', alias='__typename'
    )

--use-typed-map-values-beside-other-types¶

Type the map values of type arrays that list object beside other types.

With --use-typed-nullable-map-values, a schema whose type array lists object beside other types, such as type: [object, string] or type: [object, string, "null"], and that declares its values with additionalProperties gets typed values too, such as dict[str, int] | str, with a model for object values. Without this option those maps keep dict[str, Any], as in 0.86.0, while the maps whose type array lists object alone or with null are typed by --use-typed-nullable-map-values either way. The option changes nothing without --use-typed-nullable-map-values.

Usage

datamodel-codegen --input typed_map_values_beside_other_types.json --output-model-type pydantic_v2.BaseModel --use-typed-nullable-map-values --use-typed-map-values-beside-other-types # (1)!
  1. --use-typed-map-values-beside-other-types - the option documented here

  "title": "Settings",
  "type": "object",
  "properties": {
    "limits": {
      "type": ["object", "null"],
      "additionalProperties": {"type": "integer"}
    },
    "quotas": {
      "type": ["object", "string"],
      "additionalProperties": {"type": "integer"}
    },
    "owners": {
      "type": ["object", "string", "null"],

        "type": "object",
        "properties": {"name": {"type": "string"}}
      }

}

--use-typed-nullable-map-values¶

Type the values of nullable maps as their schemas say instead of Any.

A nullable map here is a schema whose type array lists object alone or with null, such as type: [object, "null"] or type: [object], and that declares its values with additionalProperties. Without the --use-typed-nullable-map-values flag the output keeps the 0.83.0 form, dict[str, Any] | None, or dict[str, Any] when the type array has no null, whatever the values are. A map made nullable by nullable: true and a map typed type: object keep their typed values either way. The maps of type arrays that list object beside other types, such as type: [object, string], are typed only with --use-typed-map-values-beside-other-types too.

With the flag the values follow their schema, such as dict[str, int] | None or dict[str, Player] | None, and an object value gets a model named after the map, such as Teams1 for the values of Teams. Those value models take the names left free, so the other models keep their 0.83.0 names, and options keyed by class name, such as --base-class-map or --aliases, apply to the final names. Typed values change more than the maps themselves: --reuse-model makes a value model and the models equal to it one model, which can leave out a schema's class, and no longer makes nullable maps with different values subclasses of each other, and --collapse-root-models collapses the root models that the values use. When typing the values would change the modules written, the values of the whole run stay untyped.

Usage

datamodel-codegen --input nullable_map_value_types.yaml --use-typed-nullable-map-values --output-model-type pydantic_v2.BaseModel # (1)!
  1. --use-typed-nullable-map-values - the option documented here

--use-union-operator¶

Use | operator for Union types (PEP 604).

The --use-union-operator flag generates union types using the | operator (e.g., str | None) instead of Union[str, None] or Optional[str]. This is the default behavior.

Related: --no-use-union-operator

See also: Python Version Compatibility

Usage

datamodel-codegen --input annotated.graphql --output-model-type pydantic_v2.BaseModel --use-annotated --use-union-operator # (1)!

    listField: [String!]!

    optionalListOptionalField: [String]
    listListField:[[String!]!]!
}

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Annotated, Literal

from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
from typing_extensions import TypeAliasType

Boolean = TypeAliasType("Boolean", bool)
"""
The `Boolean` scalar type represents `true` or `false`.
"""


String = TypeAliasType("String", str)
"""
The `String` scalar type represents textual data, represented as UTF-8 character sequences. The String type is most often used by GraphQL to represent free-form human-readable text.
"""


class A(BaseModel):
    field: String
    listField: list[String]
    listListField: list[list[String]]

    optionalListField: list[String] | None = None
    optionalListOptionalField: list[String | None] | None = None
    typename__: Annotated[Literal['A'] | None, Field(alias='__typename')] = 'A'

--use-unique-items-as-set¶

Generate set types for arrays with uniqueItems constraint.

The --use-unique-items-as-set flag generates Python set types instead of list types for JSON Schema arrays that have the uniqueItems constraint set to true, enforcing uniqueness at the type level.
